title: Radio Waves Power Fusion Plasma Current, Paving Way for Continuous Reactor Operation
body:
A breakthrough experiment in the United States has demonstrated that radio‑frequency waves can directly drive an electric current inside a fusion plasma, a technique known as “helicon current drive.” The result, achieved by a team led by Jeff Lestz at General Atomics in San Diego, marks the first clear evidence that this method can sustain plasma currents without relying on the traditional inductive drive used in today’s tokamak reactors. If the approach can be scaled, it could pave the way for tokamaks that operate continuously, a long‑sought milestone on the path to practical fusion power.

The experiment was conducted on the DIII‑D tokamak, a flagship device that has been upgraded over the past decade with state‑of‑the‑art magnetic confinement and diagnostic capabilities. Researchers injected a high‑frequency helicon wave—a type of low‑frequency, high‑density plasma wave—into the hot, magnetically confined deuterium‑tritium mixture. By carefully tuning the wave’s frequency and polarization, the team succeeded in transferring angular momentum from the radio waves to the charged particles, thereby generating a net toroidal current that persisted long after the external power source was turned off.

Historically, tokamaks have depended on a transformer‑like “central solenoid” to induce the plasma current, a method that inherently limits operation to short pulses. This pulsed nature forces reactors to cycle between start‑up, burn, and shutdown phases, complicating the engineering of components that must survive repeated thermal and mechanical stresses. Helicon current drive, by contrast, offers a non‑inductive route to sustain the current, potentially enabling steady‑state operation. The new data show that the helicon‑driven current reached several hundred kiloamperes—comparable to the levels needed for full‑size reactors—while maintaining plasma stability and confinement quality.

The implications extend beyond merely prolonging the burn time of a tokamak. Continuous operation would allow fusion plants to deliver a stable electricity output, smoothing the integration of fusion into existing power grids. Moreover, eliminating the massive central solenoid could reduce the size, cost, and complexity of future reactor designs. Engineers could allocate more space for breeding blankets, neutron shielding, or advanced divertor concepts, all of which are critical for achieving net‑positive energy and handling the intense neutron flux that accompanies deuterium‑tritium fusion.

Nevertheless, significant challenges remain before helicon current drive can be declared a ready‑for‑prime‑time technology. Scaling the method to the multi‑megaampere currents required for commercial reactors will demand higher power radio‑frequency systems and refined wave‑coupling strategies to avoid deleterious effects such as plasma turbulence or unwanted heating. Additionally, long‑duration experiments are needed to assess how the driven current interacts with other plasma control mechanisms, including magnetic shear, pressure profiles, and impurity transport. International collaborations are already planning to test helicon‑type waves on larger devices such as ITER and the Chinese EAST tokamak, where the higher magnetic fields and plasma volumes will provide a more stringent proving ground.

If these hurdles can be overcome, helicon current drive could become a cornerstone of the next generation of fusion reactors, shifting the paradigm from intermittent, pulsed experiments to steady‑state power plants. The General Atomics team’s success not only validates a decades‑old theoretical concept but also offers a tangible pathway toward the continuous, carbon‑free energy source that scientists and policymakers have long envisioned. As research accelerates, the fusion community will watch closely to see whether radio waves can indeed keep the heart of a tokamak beating nonstop.
